blocks.text: Collect an object's parts through a readable sequence of calls, then create it in one validated step.

A **builder** holds the mutable, in-progress state. Its `build()` method checks the invariants that span several fields and returns an **immutable** product. Callers name each value instead of passing a long positional argument list, and no half-built object ever escapes.

items: **Solves:** telescoping constructors and boolean-flag argument lists.
**Guarantees:** the product is valid and immutable once built.
**Needs:** a place for cross-field validation, which is `build()`.

walkthrough.note: The product is an immutable record. Its compact constructor guards null, and `builder(host)` is the single entry point.
The builder keeps defaults for optional fields and requires the mandatory `host` up front. Each setter returns `this` to allow chaining.
`build()` validates rules that involve several fields, like TLS on port 80. Only a consistent configuration can leave the builder.
The call site reads like a named-argument list. Only the values that differ from defaults appear.
An invalid combination fails at `build()` time with a precise message, not later inside the code that uses the config.

blocks.text: Constructing an outbound HTTP request in an API client.

A request has a method, URI, headers, a timeout, optional body and authentication. Most combinations are rare and some are illegal, such as a body on `GET` in your API. A builder exposes only the legal chain, adds headers incrementally, and rejects the illegal combinations in `build()` before anything touches the network.
Payoff: call sites document themselves, and an invalid request fails fast at one spot.

lists.title: Use when
items: A type has many optional parameters or a long constructor.
Validity depends on several fields together and must be checked once.
You want an immutable product assembled from mutable steps.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Two or three required fields: a constructor or a record is shorter.
Most fields are required: a builder only catches omissions at runtime, a constructor at compile time.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Validating in setters instead of `build()` misses cross-field rules.
Reusing one builder after `build()` can leak shared mutable state.
A mandatory field made optional lets `null` reach the product.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A builder for a two-field value object.
A director class with one caller and one recipe.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records remove the boilerplate of the product; generators such as Lombok `@Builder` or Immutables remove the builder's.
Add a `toBuilder()` or a `with...` method for copy-with-change instead of mutating.

rows.difference: Factory Method chooses which class to instantiate. Builder gathers many values for one class and checks them together.
Abstract Factory returns several products right away. Builder returns one product, after a sequence of configuration calls.
Prototype starts from a configured copy and tweaks it. Builder starts from defaults and assembles; `toBuilder()` joins the two.
Builders are a natural way to assemble Composite trees, with nested builders or `add` calls for children.
Builder is the standard way to produce an immutable object with many fields: mutate the builder, freeze the product.

options.why: Values accumulate through chained calls, and `build()` validates and returns the finished object.
No subclass or supplier decides which class to create; the focus is assembling one object's state.
Chained calls look like wrapping, but each call mutates a builder rather than wrapping an object with the same interface.
Nothing is copied from an existing instance; the object starts from `to(...)`.

exercises.scenario: A job-scheduler configuration has two required fields and eight optional ones. Some optional fields only make sense together, such as a retry count with a backoff, and the configuration should be immutable once created.

options.why: Many optional values, cross-field rules and an immutable result are exactly what a builder with a validating `build()` handles.
The difficulty is assembling and validating many values, not choosing between classes.
Copying a template helps when instances are near-identical, but here the first configuration still has to be assembled.
There is one product, not a family of related ones.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that breaks the Builder pattern.
lines: private Config(String h, int p) { this.host = h; this.port = p; }
Builder host(String h) { this.host = h; return this; }
Builder port(int p) { this.port = p; return this; }
Config build() { return new Config(host, port); }
exercises.explanation: `build()` never validates, so a `Config` with a null host or an invalid port can exist. Check `host != null` and the port range before constructing.

exercises.prompt: Explain Builder in your own words: where should validation happen, and when would you skip it?

modelAnswer.text: A builder accumulates values through named, chainable calls and creates the product only in `build()`, which validates rules that span several fields and returns an immutable object. Skip it for small types where a constructor or record already reads clearly.

keyPoints: Validation of cross-field rules lives in `build()`
Replaces telescoping constructors and flag arguments
Not worth it for two or three fields
